title: Using macOS Secure Enclave for hardware-backed SSH keys
excerpt: Store SSH private keys in the Secure Enclave and require Touch ID for every use without third-party software.
body:
A fresh macOS Sequoia laptop can hold an SSH private key inside the Secure Enclave, the isolated cryptographic coprocessor on Apple silicon. The key never touches the filesystem, and Touch ID must approve every signing request. In practice that means a malicious script that can read ~/.ssh or dump RAM still cannot steal the private material.

The walkthrough below shows how to create a non-exportable identity with sc_auth, turn that identity into a key-handle that the OpenSSH client understands, and wire the client to the built-in provider library. After the steps are complete the machine will use a hardware-backed SSH identity for everyday logins, without any deprecated flags or third-party tools.

## Create a non-exportable identity with sc_auth  

macOS ships the sc_auth utility as part of the Smart Card Authentication framework. Although the name mentions smart cards, the tool also manages CryptoTokenKit identities that live in the Secure Enclave. Running the following command creates a new signing identity:

```bash
sc_auth create-ctk-identity -l "ssh-MacBook" -k p-256-ne -t bio
```

The `-l "ssh-MacBook"` flag gives the identity a human-readable label that appears only on the local machine. The `-k p-256-ne` option selects the NIST P-256 curve and marks the key as non-exportable; the private key material is generated inside the enclave and can never be extracted. The `-t bio` flag ties every signing operation to Touch ID, so a fingerprint must be presented before the enclave will sign.

If the command fails with an error such as “Failed to generate keypair” (OSStatus -25293), the likely cause is a missing or corrupted Touch ID enrollment. Re-enrolling a fingerprint in System Settings → Touch ID & Password clears the error and the command succeeds. At this point the Secure Enclave holds a signing identity that SSH can reference later.

## Export a key-handle for SSH  

OpenSSH does not need the private key itself; it only needs a key-handle that points to the enclave-resident identity. The handle is created with ssh-keygen using the built-in keychain provider library:

```bash
ssh-keygen -w /usr/lib/ssh-keychain.dylib -K -N ""
```

When the prompt asks for a PIN, simply press Enter, biometric keys do not use a PIN. Touch ID will pop up to confirm the operation. The command writes two files in the current directory: `id_ecdsa_sk_rk`, the handle that tells SSH “ask the Secure Enclave to sign”, and `id_ecdsa_sk_rk.pub`, the public key that must be copied to `~/.ssh/authorized_keys` on every remote host. Moving the pair into the standard SSH directory completes the export step:

```bash
mv id_ecdsa_sk_rk* ~/.ssh/
```

The handle file remains only a reference; the actual private material stays sealed inside the enclave.

## Configure the SSH client to use the Secure Enclave provider  

OpenSSH looks for a library that knows how to talk to a `*_sk` key. macOS provides that library at /usr/lib/ssh-keychain.dylib. Point the client at it with an environment variable:

```bash
export SSH_SK_PROVIDER=/usr/lib/ssh-keychain.dylib
```

Add the line to the user’s shell profile (`~/.zshrc` or `~/.bashrc`) and reload the shell:

```bash
source ~/.zshrc   # or source ~/.bashrc
```

Older tutorials often suggest `ssh-add -K` to load keys from the Apple keychain. The `-K` flag is deprecated and now prints a warning. The modern approach relies on the `SSH_SK_PROVIDER` variable and the `-w` option used when the handle was created. No extra flags are required when invoking `ssh`.

## Compare native Secure Enclave with common alternatives  

When the goal is “the private key cannot be extracted even if the machine is compromised”, three approaches appear in the wild:

1. Native Secure Enclave, uses only built-in macOS tools, no extra hardware, and the key never leaves the chip.  
2. Third-party wrappers such as Secretive, add a GUI and key-management features but still depend on the same hardware.  
3. External hardware tokens such as YubiKey, provide the same non-exportable guarantee and work across platforms, but require carrying a separate device.

The native solution wins on simplicity: a single command line, no extra software to update, and no risk of losing a physical token. The trade-off is that the workflow is tied to macOS and to Touch ID; scripts that need unattended SSH access must fall back to a different key type.

For teams that already use password managers with SSH support (1Password, Bitwarden), the convenience of a shared vault may outweigh the hardware guarantee, but those solutions still decrypt the key into memory at use time. The source article notes that the author prefers the hardware-backed approach precisely because the private key is impossible to extract, even on a fully compromised Mac.

## Put the public key on remote servers  

The only step that still requires manual copying is placing `id_ecdsa_sk_rk.pub` on each host you intend to access. The command below appends the key to the remote `authorized_keys` file:

```bash
ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_ecdsa_sk_rk.pub user@remote-host
```

Because the public key is a standard ECDSA-SK format, any recent OpenSSH server accepts it without additional configuration. After the copy, a regular `ssh user@remote-host` will trigger Touch ID, the enclave will sign the challenge, and the connection will be established.

## The takeaway  

macOS Secure Enclave lets a Mac store an SSH private key that is truly non-exportable and bound to biometric approval. Use sc_auth to create the enclave identity, export a key-handle with `ssh-keygen -w`, and set `SSH_SK_PROVIDER` to the built-in library. Skip the deprecated `ssh-add -K` flag; the environment variable is the supported way to enable hardware-backed SSH on modern macOS versions. The result is a password-less login experience that keeps the private key out of reach from attackers.
